claims.text: A conventional tempered martensitic steel with controlled impurity content can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition under calibrated tempering.
Embrittling impurities such as phosphorus segregate within a narrow intermediate tempering-temperature range.
Intermediate-temperature impurity segregation dramatically reduces steel ductility.
The embrittling effect of impurity segregation is suppressed at higher temperatures.
Finely controlling tempering temperature and time can maximize grain-boundary impurity segregation within the intermediate-temperature range.
The steel is ductile at low temperatures.
Controlled temper embrittlement occurs at intermediate temperatures through impurity segregation.
Ductility is restored at higher temperatures due to enhanced dislocation activity and reduced segregation effects.
Localized impurity segregation at grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes a dramatic loss of ductility through temper embrittlement.
Limited atomic mobility at low temperatures prevents significant impurity segregation.
Increased diffusion at high temperatures mitigates the embrittlement effect and restores ductility.
The proposed treatment will produce a reproducible ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The transition will consist of high ductility at low and high temperatures and a pronounced ductility decrease within a narrow intermediate-temperature window.
Tempered martensitic steel processed without calibrated tempering control exhibits uniform ductility outside the intentionally induced embrittlement window.
The proposed effect is restricted to conventional alloys prone to temper embrittlement through impurity segregation.
The proposed effect is not applicable to compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys because they lack the asserted impurity-segregation mechanism.
